extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Catholic theology, seminarians, and clergy
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and doctrinal criteria concerning the nature, necessity, and operation of actual (prevenient and cooperating) grace in relation to salutary acts, and the Church’s condemnations of Pelagian and Semipelagian errors. Focuses on biblical, patristic, conciliar, and theological arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and classification of salutary acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Salutary acts (actus salutares) are those directed to the attainment of sanctifying grace and the supernatural end of man; they are divided into (1) those that prepare for justification (actus simpliciter salutares) and (2) those which, following justification, gain merits for Heaven (actus meritorii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are 'diametrically opposed' to acts good only in a natural way and must be carefully distinguished from natural good acts; Fathers used various phrases (e.g. agere ad salutem, agere ad iustificationem) to denote what is here called salutary acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of actual grace for all salutary acts (overarching dogma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supernatural (actual) grace is absolutely necessary for the performance of any and all acts profitable for salvation; unaided nature cannot perform such acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Scripture (e.g. John XV 'without me you can do nothing'), patristic testimony, and theological argument: salutary acts are essentially supernatural and therefore require divine assistance; regarded as a fundamental dogma of the Christian religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pelagianism condemned: inability to deny necessity of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Pelagianism denied original sin and the necessity/existence of immediate grace of the will, asserting that the human will can, by its natural powers, keep all the commandments of God and merit salvation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Church response: multiple councils condemned Pelagian positions; canonical condemnations (e.g. Carthage, Council of Ephesus, Second Council of Orange, Council of Trent) anathematize the claim that grace is given merely to make it easier to keep the commandments as if man could do them without grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis I — Prevenient grace necessary for the beginning of faith (de fide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prevenient grace is absolutely necessary not only for faith's increase but for the very beginning of faith; faith is 'the gift of God' and the first impulse to believe is an effect of prevenient grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Scripture (e.g. John VI 'No man can come to me, except the Father draw him') and Tradition; condemned Semipelagian claims that the beginning of faith is a natural act of the will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis II — Need of prevenient and cooperating grace for every salutary act (de fide)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even after receiving faith, the sinner absolutely needs prevenient and co-operating grace for every single salutary act required in the process of justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounded in conciliar definitions (Second Council of Orange; Council of Trent) and Pauline texts (Phil. II, 13); rejects Semipelagian attribution of dispositions necessary for justification to mere natural effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis III — Even in sanctifying grace actual graces are required
rubrics_metrics.description: While in the state of sanctifying grace, man still cannot perform salutary acts unless aided by actual graces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is also set forth as a matter of faith (de fide) and argued from Scripture, Tradition, and the nature of sanctifying grace which does not obviate the need for actual divine assistance in individual salutary acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of Semipelagian intermediate claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Semipelagianism taught that the beginning of faith depends on the will (initium fidei), that nature can merit grace by 'meritum de congruo', and that free-will after justification can secure final perseverance unaided; these positions were condemned by the Second Council of Orange and repudiated by the Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Church judged such compromises unacceptable; historical and patristic evidence (e.g. Augustine, earlier Fathers) is marshaled to show prevenient grace precedes any natural beginning of faith or meritorious natural disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between natural good acts and supernatural salutary acts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a clear ontological difference between acts good only in a natural way (e.g., tilling soil, acts of friendship) and salutary acts which have a supernatural end and therefore exceed natural powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theological analyses (e.g. St. Thomas) underline that acts proportioned to eternal life require a higher power (grace); this distinction is central when evaluating whether an act needs actual grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold state of man in relation to actual grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Every adult is in one of three states regarding actual grace: (1) unbelief (status infidelitatis), (2) mortal sin (status peccati mortalis), or (3) justification (status iustitiae sive gratiae sanctificantis); the need and operation of grace must be considered relative to these states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different historical errors (Pelagianism, Semipelagianism) and doctrinal conclusions are evaluated with respect to these states; the Church teaches the absolute necessity of grace in each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural and patristic warrant as criteria for doctrinal orthodoxy
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrinal claims about grace must be consistent with Scripture (e.g. John XV, Pauline pneumatology) and with the consensus or authoritative testimony of the Fathers (especially Augustine) and ecumenical/local councils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise repeatedly appeals to Scripture and Fathers as decisive evidence; novelty in denying necessity of grace is treated as indication of heresy per historical conciliar responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for evaluating theories of the supernatural character (supernaturalitas) of salutary acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories are judged on whether they make salutary acts supernatural in essence (quoad substantiam), only as to mode (quoad modum), merely per denominationem extrinsecam (Scotist), or as possessing an ontological intrinsic supernaturalitas (Suarezian view).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objections are raised to views that (a) leave nature intrinsically capable of salutary acts (untenable vs Tradition), (b) restrict supernatural character merely to mode or accident (fails to account for sanctifying grace's purpose), or (c) ground the supernatural solely in God's external acceptation. The Suarezian/ontological substantial supernaturalitas is presented as the most convincing solution, and theories must account for Tradition and the impossibility of unaided nature performing salutary acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciliar formulas and anathemas as decisive doctrinal tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertions that undermine the gratuitousness or necessity of grace (e.g. that grace is given merely to make it easier for free-will to do what it could do unaided) are subject to conciliar condemnation and anathema (e.g. canons of Carthage, Second Council of Orange, Council of Trent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing theological positions, one must compare them with explicit conciliar definitions and anathemas quoted in the text; deviation from these formulae marks error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevenient grace's differential operation on intellect and will
rubrics_metrics.description: The first judgment of credibility (iudicium credibilitatis) is determined by immediate grace of the intellect, while the subsequent affectus credulitatis springs from strengthening grace of the will; prevenient grace thus has distinct roles in intellectual assent and volitional movement toward faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This finer point addresses the moment and manner grace begins its work in the soul and provides a criterion for evaluating accounts that seek to split the beginning and increase of faith between nature and grace.
